power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Practices In Psychological Science.
This is the revised version, which has been resubmitted and is currently under review.

In their article, Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025) argue that the term "preregistration" has been used ambiguously, referring to many different components present at different stages of the research process.
text.formatted: In their article, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)</ref> argue that the term "preregistration" has been used ambiguously, referring to many different components present at different stages of the research process.

text.text: We agree with the authors' goal to "enhance understanding and support better implementation and reporting of open science" (p. 1) and that the term "preregistration" is currently being used ambiguously.
However, Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025) suggest replacing the term "preregistration", a proposal we find counterproductive.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)</ref> suggest replacing the term "preregistration", a proposal we find counterproductive.

text.text: Thus, we offer an alternative perspective on it. Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025) build on the terminology change implemented in the TOP 2025 Guidelines (Grant et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Thus, we offer an alternative perspective on it. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)</ref> build on the terminology change implemented in the TOP 2025 Guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Grant et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: TOP 2025 disaggregates preregistration into registration, study protocol, and analysis plan, and asks authors to report when each was created and shared, without taking a stance on whether "preregistration" remains useful as an umbrella term for these practices.

Going beyond this, Mayo-Wilson et al. propose that "rather than use the term 'preregistration' to refer to different times for different studies and study types, [...] authors describe specific research outputs, such as registrations, and the times at which those outputs were created and shared in relation to other relevant study events" (p. 5).

In addition, "preregistration" is not defined in the article at all, nor is it specified whether and how the other terms relate to it, implying that the authors do not see other uses for the term "preregistration".

Although the definition of preregistration has been contested, there appears to be some consensus that it requires recording a time-stamped plan for (parts of) a study before the data have been collected or examined, usually in a dedicated repository (cf. Krypotos et al., 2022; Lakens et al., 2024; Nosek et al., 2018; Parsons et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although the definition of preregistration has been contested, there appears to be some consensus that it requires recording a time-stamped plan for (parts of) a study before the data have been collected or examined, usually in a dedicated repository (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Krypotos et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Lakens et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Nosek et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Parsons et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In recent years, the term "preregistration" has become established and is now so prevalent within psychology that it can be discussed and promoted efficiently (Hardwicke & Vazire, 2024), with over a third of researchers in psychology in the Netherlands and the UK reporting that they regularly preregister their studies (Gopalakrishna et al., 2022; Silverstein et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In recent years, the term "preregistration" has become established and is now so prevalent within psychology that it can be discussed and promoted efficiently <ref type="bibr">(Hardwicke & Vazire, 2024)</ref>, with over a third of researchers in psychology in the Netherlands and the UK reporting that they regularly preregister their studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Gopalakrishna et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Silverstein et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the vast majority of published studies in psychology still include no elements that are preregistered (Hardwicke et al., 2022 (Hardwicke et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: However, the vast majority of published studies in psychology still include no elements that are preregistered <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Hardwicke et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Hardwicke et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: We worry that dropping the term will divert attention from understanding the myriad of potential benefits of the practice in its various forms, raising awareness and adoption, evaluating its impact, and proposing targeted improvements, and may ultimately cause more confusion among researchers already working on improving transparency in their research.
We agree that the different components outlined by Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025) -that is, registration, study protocol, and analysis plan -are distinct.
text.formatted: We agree that the different components outlined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)</ref> -that is, registration, study protocol, and analysis plan -are distinct.

text.text: However, distinguishing components does not require dropping the term that groups them.
For example, a protocol may or may not state hypotheses or include study materials, yet "study protocol" as an umbrella term is still useful.

Similarly, we argue that "preregistration" is a useful umbrella term to clarify that these (and other) elements of a research process can be prespecified and recorded to aid in research planning and reduce bias.

Using both the overarching term "preregistration" and terms for the specific components that can be preregistered may facilitate teaching and advocacy, while also nudging researchers to think about the utility of all possible components and the importance of being transparent about their choices.

We believe in the utility of a preregistration that includes only some of these (sub)components, as long as researchers are transparent about this and understand the relative benefits of preregistering these different elements.
Whatever researchers choose to ( not  2025) also argue for a consistent terminology across disciplines, which they believe is not achievable while using the term "preregistration".
text.formatted: Whatever researchers choose to ( <ref type="formula">not</ref>  <ref type="formula">2025</ref>) also argue for a consistent terminology across disciplines, which they believe is not achievable while using the term "preregistration".

text.text: However, we believe that an overarching framework of "preregistration" has utility in enabling interdisciplinary exchange about different goals of preregistration and how best to achieve them.

For instance, psychologists can offer lessons regarding the use of preregistration to restrict researcher degrees of freedom (e.g., Spitzer et al., 2026), while being able to learn from other disciplines how immediate public availability of preregistrations can enable the coordination of efforts and reduce the file-drawer issue (Rosenthal, 1979).
text.formatted: For instance, psychologists can offer lessons regarding the use of preregistration to restrict researcher degrees of freedom (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Spitzer et al., 2026)</ref>, while being able to learn from other disciplines how immediate public availability of preregistrations can enable the coordination of efforts and reduce the file-drawer issue <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Rosenthal, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: For this interdisciplinary exchange, resource collections like "Open Research Across Disciplines" (Farran et al., 2020; Silverstein et al., 2026) can be useful.
text.formatted: For this interdisciplinary exchange, resource collections like "Open Research Across Disciplines" <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Farran et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Silverstein et al., 2026)</ref> can be useful.

text.text: We do agree with Mayo-Wilson and colleagues that greater standardisation within disciplines makes sense.

Such efforts are currently underway in psychology to establish best-practice guidelines for various open science practices, including preregistration (see https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/).
text.formatted: Such efforts are currently underway in psychology to establish best-practice guidelines for various open science practices, including preregistration (see <ref type="url" target="https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/">https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology</ref>).

text.text: Mayo-Wilson and colleagues (2025) also suggest that the "pre" in preregistration is confusing as there is not one single event that it would precede across studies.
While this is true, we believe that this makes it even more important for authors to emphasise and specify the "pre".
To limit degrees of freedom and/or aid study planning, the practice needs to occur prior to the event relevant to that goal.
Which events are relevant may differ between study designs, as Mayo-Wilson and colleagues also point out.
For example, registration after a study's completion does not aim to reduce researchers' degrees of freedom at all, but has other benefits, e.g., findability.

At times, there is a lack of differentiation between preregistration and other types of registration, for example in the open-ended registrations on the OSF, which can convey a mistaken impression of bias control and hamper metascientific efforts (Ensinck & Lakens, 2025).
text.formatted: At times, there is a lack of differentiation between preregistration and other types of registration, for example in the open-ended registrations on the OSF, which can convey a mistaken impression of bias control and hamper metascientific efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ensinck & Lakens, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, specificity with regard to study events is already contained in most preregistration templates in psychology.

For example, the OSF Preregistration Template (https://osf.io/x5w7h/files/jea94) and the PRP-QUANT Template (Bosnjak et al., 2022; available at: https://prereg-psych.org/) ask about when the preregistration is taking place with regard to data collection, access, and analysis.
text.formatted: For example, the OSF Preregistration Template (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/x5w7h/files/jea94">https://osf.io/x5w7h/files/jea94</ref>) and the PRP-QUANT Template <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bosnjak et al., 2022</ref>; available at: <ref type="url" target="https://prereg-psych.org/">https://prereg-psych.org/</ref>) ask about when the preregistration is taking place with regard to data collection, access, and analysis.

text.text: Mayo-Wilson and colleagues state the definition of register (verb) as: "Enter a record in a register, such as submit minimum study information to ClinicalTrials.gov" (p. 2).
However, a wider definition of register (verb) is "to make a record of" (Merriam-Webster, 2026).
text.formatted: However, a wider definition of register (verb) is "to make a record of" <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Merriam-Webster, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We believe that this wider definition of register, paired with "pre" in "preregistration", captures the act of making a record of something prior to the activity relevant to that goal, and that this wider definition covers all current uses of preregistration in psychology.
We agree with Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025) that currently, platforms typically used to register studies in psychology do not live up to the highest standards.
text.formatted: We agree with <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)</ref> that currently, platforms typically used to register studies in psychology do not live up to the highest standards.

text.text: Some (pre)registration platforms are not indexed at all and offer no search (e.g., AsPredicted), others are indexed but do not require sufficient minimum information (e.g., open-ended OSF registrations), many default to embargo periods, few have robust plans for long-term preservation, and no database offers an aggregated search across multiple preregistration platforms.
Stage 1 Registered Reports, as a type of preregistration, should be included in such a registry, since they are currently not consistently registered 1 .
Yet, we do not believe that these issues are a reason to replace the term "preregistration", but rather that there is an opportunity to improve infrastructure.
Preregistration platforms and journals offering Registered Reports should work towards achieving these requirements.

For example, different preregistration platforms could collaborate to ensure long-term preservation (similar to initiatives for data repositories, e.g., DataPASS, http://data-pass.org), and to develop preregistration metadata standards (for example, to distinguish between preregistration and registration after a study is completed).
text.formatted: For example, different preregistration platforms could collaborate to ensure long-term preservation (similar to initiatives for data repositories, e.g., DataPASS, <ref type="url" target="http://data-pass.org">data-pass.org</ref>), and to develop preregistration metadata standards (for example, to distinguish between preregistration and registration after a study is completed).

text.text: Preregistration platforms should also work towards solutions to balance the benefits of immediate findability with concerns from authors about being "scooped" and about their identities being revealed in masked peer review.
There is room for different preregistration platforms to take different approaches to this issue (and others), so that authors and journals can make an informed decision about their priorities.

Ultimately, debate about the purpose, scope, and limits of preregistration can enable the development of discipline-specific and method-specific norms regarding best practices of the what, when, and where of preregistration, and support researchers in making their own reasoned choices and transparently reporting these.

We propose that for this, it is neither necessary nor desirable for the field of psychology to replace the term "preregistration" altogether; instead, we should advocate that researchers are transparent about all aspects of their preregistrations, and develop policies that enable this.

As mentioned previously, best-practice guidelines for preregistration in psychology are currently under development (https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/), which will include recommendations for preregistration reporting.
text.formatted: As mentioned previously, best-practice guidelines for preregistration in psychology are currently under development (<ref type="url" target="https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/">https://forrt.org/best-practices-psychology/</ref>), which will include recommendations for preregistration reporting.

text.text: In the meantime, to aid transparency in reporting, we propose that authors include and follow a 21-word statement, similar to the one proposed by Simmons et al. (2012) for transparent reporting of methods.
text.formatted: In the meantime, to aid transparency in reporting, we propose that authors include and follow a 21-word statement, similar to the one proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Simmons et al. (2012)</ref> for transparent reporting of methods.

text.text: Specifically, we propose that researchers state: "For each study, we clearly report what was preregistered, when, where it is available, and any deviations that occurred after preregistration."
